chapter_intro_context.source_locator: DMS3.0 printed9/PDF24 retained in final immutable span
chapter_intro_context.source_text:
Capabilities are broken into three categories. These categories cover what the component can report about itself, what
the component can report about the world, and what actions the component can perform. Informational items reported
by the component about itself are called properties. Informational items the component observed in the world are called
observables. Actions that can be performed by the component are called commands.
chapter_intro_context.review_scope: CONTEXT_ONLY; later parent-block reconciliation remains assigned. No new property review or block closure.

semantic_notes.finding: Chapter3 distinguishes component-about-itself properties, observed-world observables and available actions as commands. Identity, Position and Velocity have separate property/observable IDs. All30 index entries say modality; body chapters distinguish services and capability bins.
semantic_notes.handling: Retain category-specific IDs, body roles and immutable index metadata; do not turn all bins/services into physical modalities.

records.source_span_text:
2.0 Problems ISA Addresses
 Before considering what ISA is and the features and benefits it provides, it is important to
 understand the problems ISA addresses.

 Typical sensor systems are siloed, requiring a proprietary connection to configure their
 operation and access their data. Each sensor requires a separate, point-to-point connection,
 as well as a separate operator, reducing manpower from other tasks. The problem is
 multiplied when an area has many sensor systems in it, with no way to communicate with
 each other or contribute to a shared situational awareness.

 If a sensor is configured to work with another system, the connection must be configured
 pre-deployment and must be defined for those specific systems, with no way to
 interoperate with a future, unknown system.

 Legacy sensor systems typically operate using unsecured communication, making them
 susceptible to eavesdropping, message manipulation (reply of old messages, changing
 message content, or publishing false information), and control by an external party,
 increasing tactical risks.




                                                                                                2

records.title: Features
records.source_locator: ISA Introductory Guide6.0r2, section4.1, Features; PDFpages12-13; printed start6
records.source_span_text:
4.1      Features
 ISA is designed to be a single standard that expresses anything sensor-related in one way.
 To accomplish this goal, ISA provides the following features:

       Data definitions using a comprehensive specification. The data specification
        enables systems, even ones that have never been integrated with each other
        previously, to exchange data in a common format, without requiring additional
        onsite modifications, translators, or other system adaptations.

       Dynamic discovery of assets on the network, without prior knowledge or
        ownership. As a result, a system need only be configured to talk to a single
        connection point (in ISA parlance, the Controller), which then manages the creation
        and maintenance of a virtual network to exchange information with other systems.

       Dynamic discovery of sensor data on the network. Because the data is well-
        defined, sensors can define what they can provide (sensor information), and
        operators/systems can specify what information they need. The ISA virtual
        network—using its connection points, or Controllers—exchanges data regarding
        information needs (subscriptions) and sources (publications) and seamlessly
        connects sources with needs to dynamically satisfy operator information requests.
        Operators, in turn, can be alerted to items of interest. Live data can also be stored
        and made available for querying later, as historical data.

       Integration of many assets into a common display. Using information supplied
        by the ISA virtual network, Command and Control (C2) elements can determine
        what information is available and support operators' requests and displays of the
        resulting, tailored information. Operators can see what all of the sensors and all of
        the capabilities are, giving them a full picture of the battlefield and enhanced
        situational awareness.




                                                                                                6
       Tasking of assets. ISA provides services to enable operators to specify tasks to be
       performed, such as changing the direction of sensing or the location to observe,
       toggling the functional modes to be used (i.e., visible versus infrared), and triggering
       specific actions (i.e., get a range from a laser range finder). Systems can also choose
       to use cooperative services to determine request priorities and sensor ownerships.
       For example, an operator can reserve one or more sensors for a period of time, but
       that reservation can be managed and changed dynamically, if circumstances change.

native_rules: The source presents one common specification for exchanging sensor-related data among systems, including systems not previously integrated.
A system is configured to communicate with a Controller; the Controller manages a virtual network for information exchange.
Sensors describe information they can provide, while operators/systems describe their information needs.
Controllers exchange information about sources/publications and needs/subscriptions to connect the two.
Live data can also be stored for later historical querying; this is described as a capability, not a mandatory storage guarantee.
C2 display functions use network-supplied information about assets, capabilities and requested results.
Tasking supports specifying actions or modes. Cooperative services may determine request priorities and sensor ownership/reservation arrangements.
An operator may reserve one or more sensors for a period, and that reservation may change dynamically.

No actual discovery, storage, successful task, authorization decision or physical effect was observed by this guide.

The no-additional-translator claim concerns integration through the common specification; it is not evidence that every legacy device is natively ISA-capable or that adapters cannot exist (section6.1 explicitly lists adapters).

5.0 Benefits of ISA
 ISA provides the following benefits:

       Reduces burden on the warfighter.

       Provides quicker, more efficient mission execution.

       Allows for improved situational awareness, from the tactical edge to the command
        post.

       Enables sensor to shooter scenarios.

       Operates on, and across, all security enclaves.

       Integrates into existing networks and C2 systems.

       Works with any sensor modality (EOIR, CBRN, ELINT, UGS, etc.).

       Enables processing of data near the point of collection.

       Supports networks from Degraded Denied Intermittent Limited to enterprise.

       Uses the latest encryption for security.

       Supports authorization of actions.

       Provides the material solution for Sensor CE and is part of the Army COE.

records.title: Overview
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 1.0 Overview; PDF 8
records.source_span_text:
1.0 Overview
 Typical sensor systems require a proprietary connection to configure their operation and
 access their data. Each sensor requires a separate, point-to-point connection, as well as a
 separate operator, reducing manpower from other tasks. The problem is multiplied when
 an area has many sensor systems in it, with no way to communicate with each other or
 contribute to a shared situational awareness.

 If a sensor is configured to work with another system, the connection must be configured
 pre-deployment and must be defined for those specific systems, with no way to
 interoperate with a future, unknown system. In addition, as either system within the
 connection changes, maintenance is required to update, revalidate, and redeliver one or
 both systems making the connection. With ISA, only the system making the change needs to
 perform maintenance and only to revalidate their ISA behaviors – other systems are not
 impacted because the ISA standard isolates the change from propagating to other ISA-
 enabled systems.

 Legacy sensor systems typically operate using unsecured communication, making them
 susceptible to eavesdropping, message manipulation (reply of old messages, changing
 message content, or publishing false information), and control by an external party,
 increasing tactical risks.




                                                                                               1

records.title: The ISA Standard
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 2.0 The ISA Standard; PDF 9,10,11
records.source_span_text:
2.0 The ISA Standard

2.1       Overview
 The Integrated Sensor Architecture (ISA) is an interoperability solution that allows for the
 sharing of information between sensors and systems in a dynamic, tactical environment.


 Figure 1 - An Example of an ISA Scenario




2.2       Features
 ISA is designed to be a single standard that expresses anything sensor-related in one way.
 To accomplish this goal, ISA provides the following features:

        Data definitions using a comprehensive specification. The data specification
         enables systems, even ones that have never been integrated with each other


                                                                                                2
     previously, to exchange data in a common format, without requiring additional
    onsite modifications, translators, or other system adaptations.

   Dynamic discovery of assets on the network, without prior knowledge or
    ownership. As a result, a system need only be configured to talk to a single
    connection point (in ISA parlance, the Controller), which then manages the creation
    and maintenance of a virtual network to exchange information with other systems.

   Dynamic discovery of sensor data on the network. Because the data is well-
    defined, sensors can define what they can provide (sensor information), and
    operators/systems can specify what information they need. The ISA virtual
    network—using its connection points, or Controllers—exchanges data regarding
    information needs (subscriptions) and sources (publications) and seamlessly
    connects sources with needs to dynamically satisfy operator information requests.
    Operators, in turn, can be alerted to items of interest. Live data can also be stored
    and made available for querying later, as historical data.

   Integration of many assets into a common display. Using information supplied
    by the ISA virtual network, Command and Control (C2) elements can determine
    what information is available and support operators' requests and displays of the
    resulting, tailored information. Operators can see what all of the sensors and all of
    the capabilities are, giving them a full picture of the battlefield and enhanced
    situational awareness.

   Tasking of assets. ISA provides services to enable operators to specify tasks to be
    performed, such as changing the direction of sensing or the location to observe,
    toggling the functional modes to be used (i.e., visible versus infrared), and triggering
    specific actions (i.e., get a range from a laser range finder). Systems can also choose
    to use cooperative services to determine request priorities and sensor ownerships.
    For example, an operator can reserve one or more sensors for a period of time, but
    that reservation can be managed and changed dynamically, if circumstances change.




                                                                                              3
 2.3     Benefits
ISA provides the following benefits:

      Reduces burden on the warfighter.

      Provides quicker, more efficient mission execution.

      Allows for improved situational awareness, from the tactical edge to the command
       post.

      Enables sensor to shooter scenarios.

      Operates on, and across, all security enclaves.

      Integrates into existing networks and C2 systems.

      Works with any sensor modality (EOIR, CBRN, ELINT, UGS, etc.).

      Enables processing of data near the point of collection.

      Supports networks from Degraded Denied Intermittent Limited to enterprise.

      Uses the latest encryption for security.

      Supports authorization of actions.

      Provides the material solution for Sensor CE and is part of the Army COE.




                                                                                          4

records.title: Features
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 2.2 Features; PDF 9,10
records.source_span_text:
2.2       Features
 ISA is designed to be a single standard that expresses anything sensor-related in one way.
 To accomplish this goal, ISA provides the following features:

        Data definitions using a comprehensive specification. The data specification
         enables systems, even ones that have never been integrated with each other


                                                                                                2
     previously, to exchange data in a common format, without requiring additional
    onsite modifications, translators, or other system adaptations.

   Dynamic discovery of assets on the network, without prior knowledge or
    ownership. As a result, a system need only be configured to talk to a single
    connection point (in ISA parlance, the Controller), which then manages the creation
    and maintenance of a virtual network to exchange information with other systems.

   Dynamic discovery of sensor data on the network. Because the data is well-
    defined, sensors can define what they can provide (sensor information), and
    operators/systems can specify what information they need. The ISA virtual
    network—using its connection points, or Controllers—exchanges data regarding
    information needs (subscriptions) and sources (publications) and seamlessly
    connects sources with needs to dynamically satisfy operator information requests.
    Operators, in turn, can be alerted to items of interest. Live data can also be stored
    and made available for querying later, as historical data.

   Integration of many assets into a common display. Using information supplied
    by the ISA virtual network, Command and Control (C2) elements can determine
    what information is available and support operators' requests and displays of the
    resulting, tailored information. Operators can see what all of the sensors and all of
    the capabilities are, giving them a full picture of the battlefield and enhanced
    situational awareness.

   Tasking of assets. ISA provides services to enable operators to specify tasks to be
    performed, such as changing the direction of sensing or the location to observe,
    toggling the functional modes to be used (i.e., visible versus infrared), and triggering
    specific actions (i.e., get a range from a laser range finder). Systems can also choose
    to use cooperative services to determine request priorities and sensor ownerships.
    For example, an operator can reserve one or more sensors for a period of time, but
    that reservation can be managed and changed dynamically, if circumstances change.




                                                                                              3

records.title: ISA Organization Structure
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 3.0 ISA Organization Structure; PDF 12,13
records.source_span_text:
3.0 ISA Organization Structure

3.1      Management
 ISA is managed within the PEO Intelligence, Electronic Warfare & Sensors (IEW&S)
 Integration Directorate. The Integration Directorate is focused on developing
 interoperability and convergence efforts within the PEO.


3.2      Systems Engineering
 ISA Systems Engineering (SE) develops requirements for general-purpose components and
 interfaces, architectural views of ISA networks and information exchanges, and
 cybersecurity compliance implementation rules, data markings, and supporting artifacts. In
 addition, ISA SE provides system and architectural design advisement and customer
 support involving data mappings between ISA and other standards, bridge and translator
 specification, and support for new system designs using ISA for data exchanges.


3.3      Development
 ISA has a team of software developers who maintain the core ISA SDK software, services,
 APIs, and schemas. The ISA developers are also available to provide integration consulting
 and software development services for external stakeholders.


3.4      Help Desk
 The ISA Help Desk team acts as liaisons between the ISA community and the ISA team
 members. The Help Desk facilitates gaining access to the ISA materials, provides technical
 support to ISA users, and tracks community feedback and issue reports.


3.5      Testing
 The ISA test team works to perform user-level, functional testing of each new software
 release before it is made available to the user community. The test team also works to




                                                                                              5
 reproduce issue reports received by the Help Desk and to assist the developers in
validating the implementation of software requirements.


3.6     Data Model
ISA defines a standard data model that provides a common format for information
exchange and enables dynamic discovery of data and capabilities. To update the standard,
maintain compatibility, and ensure interoperability, the ISA Data Model Team board
discusses and decides on proposed changes or additions to the ISA Data Model. The team
also supports customer needs regarding the ISA data model, including clarifying the
application, enhancement, and standardization of data elements and content usage. The
team is cross-functional, comprising members from the Systems Engineering,
Development, Help Desk, and Testing teams.


3.7     Cybersecurity
Security is a core design goal of ISA, and to ensure ISA follows the latest cybersecurity
baselines, policies, processes, and standards, ISA has a Cyber Team whose primary purpose
is ensuring that the ISA software, documentation, and processes adhere to the
requirements and policies specified by the National Institute of Standards and Technology
(NIST) and the Department of Defense (DoD).




                                                                                            6

records.title: ISA Products
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 4.0 ISA Products; PDF 14,15
records.source_span_text:
4.0 ISA Products

4.1         SDK
 The ISA SDK provides a complete package containing documentation, software, and
 schemas for use by engineers to accelerate the process of ISA integration.


4.2         Controller
 The Controller is the core of an ISA network. It is a software component that provides a
 connection point for ISA clients, offers access to ISA services, routes network traffic, and
 establishes the greater network topology.


4.3         Services
 ISA uses a software service model, where various software services are deployed to
 provide ISA functionality. The core services are provided in the ISA Controller. These
 include:

       The Communication Service – Accepts connections from client components and
        routes traffic to other components or Controllers.

       The Live Data Service – Provides access to information published by components
        through subscription and discovery.

       The Authorization Service – Allows and disallows access to the network, to ISA
        services, or to actions that can be performed by a component on the network.

 Additional services may be made available in other configurations. A primary example is
 the Historical Data Service, which records ISA network traffic for later querying and
 retrieval.


4.4         APIs
 To facilitate implementing the standards, protocols, behaviors, and data model that define
 an ISA component interface, ISA provides access to several client Application Programming


                                                                                                7
 Interfaces, or APIs. These APIs are software libraries that decrease integration time by
automatically handling the majority of the lower-level logic necessary for an ISA
component interface, allowing a developer to instead focus on implementing system-
specific functionality. ISA APIs are currently provided for the Java, C++, C#, and Python
programming languages.


4.5     Integration Tools
The ISA SDK includes several integration tools intended to assist with testing an ISA
component interface:

      Diagnostics – Connects to an ISA Controller and allows a user to view the network
       topology and inspect and export message contents.

      Visual Tool – Provides a map-based interface that enables a user to view ISA
       components in their geographical representations.

      Data Generator – Publishes information that can be discovered or received in
       subscription. Certain configurations can also receive and perform commands.

      Compliance Tool – Tests a client component interface to verify adherence to the
       ISA specification and requirements.




                                                                                            8

records.title: ISA Development
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 5.0 ISA Development; PDF 16,17,18
records.source_span_text:
5.0 ISA Development

5.1      Development Practices
 The ISA SDK is developed in response to ever-evolving use cases, security posture
 requirements, and changing technologies. Updates are carefully chosen with security,
 backwards compatibility, and low end-user impact at the forefront. Once designed, updates
 are developed iteratively in a continuous build environment, with reproducible artifacts,
 automated regression tests, test coverage analysis, and static security analysis. Release
 candidates are then subject to a rigorous hands-on test cycle before publication to the user
 base.


5.2      Testing
 When a software release candidate is available, the ISA testing team examines it from the
 perspective of an ISA user, performing functional and regression testing and reviewing the
 documentation updates to ensure they adequately explain the complexity of the software.
 Any issues found are reported in a ticketing system, shared with the developers, and
 tracked until they are mitigated and verified resolved.




                                                                                                9
 5.3     Security
ISA is developed in keeping with current Department of Defense and Department of the
Army standards for cybersecurity and software assurance.

      Cybersecurity requirements focus on "the prevention of damage to, protection of,
       and restoration of computers, electronic communications systems, electronic
       communications services, wire communication, and electronic communication,
       including information contained therein, to ensure its availability, integrity,
       authentication, confidentiality, and non-repudiation."

      Software Assurance requirements focus on "the level of confidence that software is
       free from vulnerabilities, either intentionally designed into the software or
       accidentally inserted at any time during its lifecycle, and that software functions in
       the intended manner."

In keeping these requirements at the center of the development process, the ISA Team
ensures software security through a Secure Software Development Lifecycle that ensures
security is built into its strategies, designs, development environment, work processes,
supply chain management, and all other day-to-day operations. This includes providing a
Secure Development Environment, with vetted personnel, coding management, test
management, identity and access management (IAM), and supply chain risk management
(SCRM); Cybersecurity and Assurance Capabilities, with software updates and patching,
implementing encryption, and building in logging and monitoring; and Secure Lifecycle
Management, with weakness and vulnerability management, rigorous and persistent
cybersecurity testing, and configuration control.

The ISA Team also anticipates the requirements of implementing teams and their security
authorization boundaries, and adheres to the following Department of Defense-mandated
baselines and requirements for software security, providing artifacts to the implementing
teams and allowing for least effort in achieving security approval for implementing ISA:

      Application Security Development (ASD) Security Technical Implementation Guide
       (STIG)




                                                                                                10
       NIST Special Publication 800-53r4 Security Controls - Assess Only Baseline and
       Classified Overlay

      Source Code Analysis Scans and Reports


Figure 2 - DoD DevSecOps




                                                                                        11

6.0 Community Engagement

6.1      Adoption of ISA
ISA was initially adopted by US Army organizations but has since expanded to other
branches and even coalition organizations. ISA integrations have involved systems from
various domains and capabilities, from Electronic Warfare (EW) to CBRN, aviation to
ground vehicles, seaborne systems, and more.

                   USMC
Space

PEO Simulation,
Training, and      British Army
Instrumentation




OGA, including

DTRA, CBP, and
NGA




                          13
 6.2      Data Model Enhancement

6.2.1      Data Model Additions
In order to preserve over-the-wire compatibility, the ISA data model will not change
outside of major ISA revisions. Due to the nature of the ISA data model, it is possible to
create custom properties, observables and commands within the standard ISA data model.
To help standardize these custom data elements(s), the ISA team has created a process
where the ISA Data Model Team (DMT) reviews and approves commonly-used data model
additions to ensure interoperability between users. These additions will be documented on
the community website and will eventually transition into a future version of the ISA data
model.

The ISA team has defined three different levels of acceptance:

        Custom – Not formally recognized by the ISA DMT. Entries with this marking are
         provided only for general awareness.

        Nominated – Under consideration for standardization. Entries with this marking
         have been reviewed by the ISA DMT. Feedback from communities of interest is
         welcomed. This content may change as it is reviewed by a wider audience.

        Accepted – Suggested for use as appropriate. Entries with this marking are
         expected to transition to the standard data model in a future major release.

An approved addition is formally included in the ISA data model and added to the Data
Model Specification in the first version after incorporating it.

In addition to ongoing development work, specific community data model additions have
been made:

        CBRN

        Video Analytics

These data model community additions are included in the main Data Model Specification.




                                                                                             14
 6.2.2     Data Model Process
Data model suggestions from the community are proposed, evaluated, and can be accepted
into the standard ISA data model, using the following process:

   1. The ISA Data Model Team meets periodically to discuss how to best apply the
        current data model in particular situations mentioned by ISA users (through Help
        Desk questions).

   2. If the current data model contents are not sufficient to cover one or more particular
        use case(s), data model changes can be proposed by the community and/or
        documented by the Data Model Team. The Data Model Team will review the changes
        to decide whether to incorporate them or not.

   3. If the data model changes are provisionally accepted for standardization by the Data
        Model Team, they will be prepared for the data model and be flagged as Nominated
        for a period of time (typically one year), during which community feedback will be
        taken and revisions may be made.

   4. After the one-year period, Nominated changes that have passed Data Model Team
        and community review will be finalized and graduate to Accepted status, which
        means that they will become standard in the next major data model release.

Data Model questions and feedback are gathered from correspondence to the ISA Help
Desk.


6.3     Summit
The ISA Summit is an annual event designed to bring together stakeholders from across the
varied communities of interest to learn what is going on with ISA, drive future
requirements, and foster relationships and opportunities for collaboration across
organizations and projects. It is held each year in northern Virginia and is attended by over
100 members of the ISA community from Government and industry.




                                                                                             15

records.title: Data Model Additions
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 6.2.1 Data Model Additions; PDF 21
records.source_span_text:
6.2.1      Data Model Additions
In order to preserve over-the-wire compatibility, the ISA data model will not change
outside of major ISA revisions. Due to the nature of the ISA data model, it is possible to
create custom properties, observables and commands within the standard ISA data model.
To help standardize these custom data elements(s), the ISA team has created a process
where the ISA Data Model Team (DMT) reviews and approves commonly-used data model
additions to ensure interoperability between users. These additions will be documented on
the community website and will eventually transition into a future version of the ISA data
model.

The ISA team has defined three different levels of acceptance:

        Custom – Not formally recognized by the ISA DMT. Entries with this marking are
         provided only for general awareness.

        Nominated – Under consideration for standardization. Entries with this marking
         have been reviewed by the ISA DMT. Feedback from communities of interest is
         welcomed. This content may change as it is reviewed by a wider audience.

        Accepted – Suggested for use as appropriate. Entries with this marking are
         expected to transition to the standard data model in a future major release.

An approved addition is formally included in the ISA data model and added to the Data
Model Specification in the first version after incorporating it.

In addition to ongoing development work, specific community data model additions have
been made:

        CBRN

        Video Analytics

These data model community additions are included in the main Data Model Specification.

records.title: Data Model Process
records.source_locator: ISA White Paper 6.0r2, 31 October 2023, section 6.2.2 Data Model Process; PDF 22
records.source_span_text:
6.2.2     Data Model Process
Data model suggestions from the community are proposed, evaluated, and can be accepted
into the standard ISA data model, using the following process:

   1. The ISA Data Model Team meets periodically to discuss how to best apply the
        current data model in particular situations mentioned by ISA users (through Help
        Desk questions).

   2. If the current data model contents are not sufficient to cover one or more particular
        use case(s), data model changes can be proposed by the community and/or
        documented by the Data Model Team. The Data Model Team will review the changes
        to decide whether to incorporate them or not.

   3. If the data model changes are provisionally accepted for standardization by the Data
        Model Team, they will be prepared for the data model and be flagged as Nominated
        for a period of time (typically one year), during which community feedback will be
        taken and revisions may be made.

   4. After the one-year period, Nominated changes that have passed Data Model Team
        and community review will be finalized and graduate to Accepted status, which
        means that they will become standard in the next major data model release.

Data Model questions and feedback are gathered from correspondence to the ISA Help
Desk.

records.title: Document Scope
records.source_span_text:
1.1       Document Scope
 The Integrated Sensor Architecture (ISA) is an interoperability layer for achieving
 communication between networked devices, algorithms, and user interfaces in a tactical
 domain. The goal of ISA is to enable soldiers and systems to flexibly access and use the data
 and capabilities needed to achieve operational success.

 This document provides a detailed technical description of ISA. It presents the system and
 deployment architectures employed by ISA to target the tactical operating environment.
 The document describes the services for ISA 6.0 and how they relate to each other
 architecturally. Lastly, the document details the messages specified for ISA and how the
 messages are used to perform the various required and optional behaviors defined for ISA.

 The ISA Component Requirements document presents the requirements that must be met
 for ISA. It contains requirements exclusive to ISA functionality and requirements for all
 ISA-compliant components.

 The low-level details for how to interface with ISA are captured in the ISA Interface Control
 Document (ICD) and ISA Data Model Specification (DMS). The ICD addresses the
 communication protocols and technologies for achieving secure connections between ISA-
 compliant components and establishing the presentation format to be used over a
 connection. The DMS documents the content of the messages exchanged over these
 connections.
records.meaning: Defines the SDD as the technical description of ISA system/deployment architecture, service relationships and message behaviors, with separate requirements and interface/data specifications retaining their own authority.
native_rules: ISA is described as an interoperability layer among networked devices, algorithms and user interfaces in a tactical domain.
The SDD covers system/deployment architectures, the services of ISA 6.0 and the required/optional message behaviors.
The Component Requirements document contains requirements for ISA functionality and ISA-compliant components.
The ICD addresses connection protocols, technologies and presentation-format establishment; the DMS describes message content.
limitations: The statement of goals and architecture does not establish interoperability test results, universal DIM classes or a chosen CSAPI/SensorML binding.
This block is not a substitute for the later assigned Component Requirements, Controller Requirements or ICD reviews.
Devices, algorithms and user interfaces are possible interacting subjects; the text does not equate an ISA component with one physical device or one OS process.

records.title: Design Tenets
records.source_span_text:
3.0 Design Tenets
 ISA is a software-only solution; it is not deployed with its own hardware elements. Instead,
 ISA leverages and relies on hardware-based capabilities provided on the platforms on/in
 which ISA resides, namely:

    •   Networking – ISA relies on the presence of wired and wireless networks and
        network infrastructure to deliver data/information.

    •   Computing – To meet its computing needs, ISA leverages computing hardware that
        are available on a platform or that are part of an integrating system.

    •   Time source – The time used by ISA must be synchronized for proper operation. ISA
        is dependent on the existence of an authoritative time source on platforms (e.g.,
        Global Positioning System (GPS) receivers) to achieve synchronized time.

 As a software solution that relies on networks, ISA is heavily influenced by design tenets
 considered best practices for software-based, network-centric solutions. Key design tenets
 for ISA are:

    •   Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) – Functionality is provided as a service, which
        is a self-contained collection of related capabilities and behaviors that supports a
        specified interface. ISA is architected as a group of services, each having a well-
        defined interface. The definition of an ISA service is a combination of the
        requirements for the service, as specified in the ISA Controller Requirements
        document, and the data model elements exchanged for the service, as documented
        in the ISA DMS. Services can be dynamically added and removed. Being an SOA
        enables ISA to maximize software modularity and reuse, which in turn increases
        solution extensibility and deployment flexibility and reduces development and
        integration cost and time. The ISA services defined for ISA 6.0 are presented in
        Section 5.0, Services.

    •   Self-describing – ISA dynamically describes its capabilities, including services, and
        requires ISA-using systems to do the same. Being self-describing enables




                                                                                                6
     components to make use of the capabilities without pre-existing knowledge of the
    component itself or what type of component it is. Components describe what they
    can do, not who or what they are. This approach dramatically reduces deployment
    effort by eliminating the need to configure a component to use other specific
    components. It also achieves extreme flexibility in which components are leveraged
    as they come and go on the battlefield. Lastly, the approach facilitates the
    deployment of services, where the actual services offered for a particular
    deployment are subject to mission needs.

•   Network-agnostic – While ISA is a network-centric solution, it is network-agnostic,
    meaning that it is not aware of the particular network, or even type of network, that
    is being used to transport the data/information that it sends and receives. Being
    network-agnostic enables ISA to be flexible in terms of where it gets deployed and
    what new network technologies are established over time. Note that being network-
    agnostic does NOT mean that ISA should not be aware of the state of a particular
    network, which ISA intends to use in the future to govern the amount of traffic that
    it outputs.




                                                                                            7
records.meaning: Describes ISA as a software-only interoperability solution relying on platform networking, computing and synchronized authoritative time, and explains service orientation, self-description and network independence.
native_rules: ISA is not deployed with its own hardware; it relies on networking infrastructure and computing resources supplied by the platform or integrating system.
The time used by ISA must be synchronized for proper operation; an authoritative platform time source is assumed, with GPS receivers given as an example.
Services have specified interfaces; a service definition combines Controller Requirements and DMS data-model elements, and services can be dynamically added or removed.
Self-description emphasizes capability discovery without pre-existing knowledge of the particular component or component type.
Network-agnostic means independence from the network or network technology used for transport, not a prohibition on awareness of network state.
limitations: Software-only applies to the ISA solution. It does not assert that every represented device or composition member is software, or that each component is exactly one operating-system process.
GPS is an example, not a mandated receiver, timing algorithm, tolerance, uncertainty value or metrological traceability claim.
The self-description phrase about describing what components can do does not erase the already reviewed identity, component identifier or provenance information.
Modularity, flexibility, cost and integration-effort benefits are source design claims, not measured results for the controlled cases.
Future use of network state to govern traffic is not an implemented behavior established by this section.

records.title: Architecture Drivers
records.source_span_text:
4.1       Architecture Drivers
 Several quality attributes of the ISA architecture were driven by the severe technical
 constraints imposed by the tactical operating environment that is targeted by ISA. The
 tactical environment commonly leverages Denied Disconnected Intermittent Limited
 (DDIL) networks, which suffer from low bandwidth, indeterminate connectivity, and high
 packet loss/corruption, drastically hampering communications between platforms.
 Furthermore, the tactical environment is characterized by high platform mobility and
 disablement.

 The following ISA quality attributes had a particularly dramatic impact on the ISA
 architecture (see Appendix A, ISA Quality Attributes, for all quality attributes relevant to
 ISA):

    •    Fault tolerant – In a tactical environment, access to another platform is never
         guaranteed and will change often, especially at lower echelons, where platform
         mobility, degraded communications, and platform damage are common. The need to
         deal with dynamic conditions caused the ISA design to follow a distributed
         architecture, entailing the placement of the same ISA functionality on many
         platforms. As a result, the loss of availability of any given ISA instance in a
         deployment would not inherently prevent access to ISA.

    •    Autonomous – Because access to another platform is never guaranteed in a tactical
         operating environment, ISA is designed to be self-contained and independent. Each
         instance of ISA functionality is able to fully support local components from an
         interoperability perspective.

 One of ISA’s fundamental operational requirements is to achieve full SA. This requirement
 dictates that components providing ISA functionality be able to interconnect in order to



                                                                                                8
 enable wide-scale access to reported information and published data. Such interconnection
also enables tasking of components that are remote from the requesting system, which is
critical for SA and the execution of certain missions.
records.meaning: Explains why a constrained, mobile operating environment motivated distributed, locally autonomous ISA functionality and interconnection for broader information access.
native_rules: The targeted environment is described as using DDIL networks with constrained bandwidth, uncertain connectivity and packet loss/corruption, together with mobile or disabled platforms.
Fault tolerance is addressed architecturally by distributing the same ISA functionality across platforms.
Autonomy means an instance can support its local components from the interoperability perspective when access to another platform is unavailable.
Interconnection supports access to reported information and published data and tasking of remote components.
limitations: These are operating assumptions and design reasons, not measured availability, loss rates, guaranteed failover, guaranteed situational awareness or validated mission outcomes.
Autonomous refers to local interoperability support; it is not evidence of autonomous sensing decisions, self-governance or physical independence.
Distribution and interconnection are software deployment/network relationships, not physical part-of relationships.

records.title: ISA Components
records.source_span_text:
4.2.1     ISA Components
As mentioned above, ISA exposes and organizes its capabilities as a set of services. ISA
services that are required to be part of every ISA deployment are termed core ISA services,
and services that are not required to be part of every deployment are termed optional ISA
services. The services for ISA 6.0 are presented in Section 5.0, Services.

ISA services are provided and used by ISA components. An ISA component is a component
that complies with the ISA interface and supports the required ISA capabilities and
behaviors. An ISA interface is the combination of communication protocols, security
technologies, data encodings, and messages defined for ISA. The ISA interface is specified in
the combination of the ISA ICD (protocols, technologies, encodings) and ISA DMS
(messages).

An ISA component that provides core ISA services is called an ISA Controller. For ISA 6.0,
every ISA Controller must support all of the core ISA services (this constraint might be
relaxed in a future release), though a particular service may or may not be activated in a
given ISA Controller. Any ISA component may provide one or more of the optional ISA
services defined for ISA 6.0. Section 5.0, Services, describes the ISA services.

A collection of connected ISA components is termed an ISA network. ISA networks are
virtual networks, relying on existing physical networks (wired and wireless) for
communication. An ISA component joins an ISA network by connecting to an ISA
Controller. The ISA components use ISA services and communicate with other ISA
components via this Controller. ISA Controllers can connect to each other, expanding the
scope of an ISA network and thereby enabling wider-scale sharing of data/information and
broader access to systems for control purposes.



                                                                                              9
 Following the client/server communication paradigm, when initiating a connection, an ISA
component is said to be playing the client-side role for the connection, and the non-
initiating component is said to be playing the server-side role. Every ISA component
supports the client-side role, since every ISA component must be able to initiate a
connection to an ISA Controller. ISA Controllers also support the server-side role, since
Controllers accept connections from other ISA components (including other ISA
Controllers). The client-side role is specified in the ISA Component Requirements
document, while the server-side role is specified in the ISA Controller Requirements
document.

Figure 1 illustrates ISA components and their relationships.


Figure 1 - ISA Components
records.meaning: Defines ISA components through interface/capability/behavior support, Controllers through core-service responsibility, and virtual networks through connected components, with client/server roles assigned per connection.
native_rules: Core services are required in each deployment; optional services are not required in every deployment.
An ISA component complies with the ISA interface and supports required capabilities and behaviors.
The ISA interface combines protocols, security technologies, encodings and messages; the ICD specifies the former technical aspects and the DMS the messages.
For ISA 6.0 every Controller must support all core services, though a particular service may or may not be activated. Any ISA component may provide optional services.
The ISA network is a virtual network of connected ISA components using existing wired or wireless physical networks.
A component joins by connecting to a Controller and uses services and communicates with other components through that Controller. Controllers can interconnect to expand the network.
The connection initiator has the client-side role; the non-initiator has the server-side role.
Every component supports initiating connections to a Controller. Controllers additionally support accepting connections from components, including other Controllers.
Client-side requirements belong to Component Requirements and server-side requirements to Controller Requirements.
limitations: Core support is not identical to activation or successful use; optional service support does not turn every provider into a Controller.
Controller and client are not necessarily disjoint component classes: a Controller also supports client-side connections.
Neither service-instance count nor the boxes in Figure 1 establish hardware count or one operating-system process per component.
A virtual ISA network is distinct from the virtual ISA component term used for a non-ISA member exposed by a CIC.
The architecture does not prove a live deployed topology, particular transport/encoding selection, current authentication or conformance of any case component.

records.title: ISA Compositions
records.source_span_text:
4.2.2      ISA Compositions
An ISA composition is a collection of components that interoperates with a (broader) ISA
network via a single ISA component. An ISA composition is an integration approach that
could be employed for purposes such as exposing elements of a complex system and
exposing the capabilities of components that do not support the ISA interface.

The ISA component through which an ISA composition communicates with an ISA network
is herein said to be playing the role of a CIC in this context. A CIC could be an ISA Controller
but does not need to be.

The components other than the CIC that comprise the composition are termed composition
members. A composition member may or may not be an ISA component. If it is an ISA
component, the composition member would communicate with the CIC via the ISA




                                                                                               10
 interface. If it is not an ISA component, the composition member would communicate with
the CIC via an interface that is native to the member.

The CIC serves as the access point for all capabilities provided by the composition that are
exposed to the ISA network, including tasks that can be requested, observation data that
can be published, and property information that can be reported. Composition-level
capabilities may be formed by combining the individual capabilities of the CIC and
composition members. Hence, the capabilities provided by the composition include
composition-level capabilities and the capabilities provided individually by the CIC and
members.

Regardless of whether a composition member is an ISA component, a CIC could expose a
member’s capabilities to an ISA network with or without making the member’s existence
visible to the network. Making a member’s existence visible entails announcing the
availability of the member, declaring the member’s capabilities, and periodically reporting
the member’s status. The CIC communicates data/information for/from a visible
composition member as originating at the member. In contrast, when a composition
member’s existence is made opaque, the CIC does not announce the member and
represents any exposed capabilities for the member as being provided by the CIC.

When a composition member that is not an ISA component is made visible by a CIC, the
member is said to be a virtual ISA component, since the component “looks” like a
conformant ISA component to the ISA network. A virtual ISA component is assigned an ISA
identifier that includes the ISA identifier of its CIC, thereby associating the member with
the CIC.

For a given task request received from outside the composition, a CIC may act as a
performer by directly executing the task, a broker by actively tasking composition
members, or a relay by forwarding the request to the targeted member (either via the ISA
interface or a native interface). By definition, only visible members can be targeted from
outside the composition. When a CIC enables a visible composition member to be tasked,
the member is considered to be transparent. When a CIC does not enable a visible
composition member to be tasked, the member is considered to be translucent.




                                                                                               11
 Figure 2 illustrates the elements of an ISA composition and the varying degrees of visibility
of members.


Figure 2 - ISA Composition
records.meaning: Defines composition as an integration collection represented through a CIC, separating member conformance, member visibility, source attribution, virtual representation, taskability and the CIC’s per-request mediation role.
native_rules: A composition communicates with a broader ISA network through a single ISA component acting as CIC; the CIC may be a Controller but need not be.
Every other component in the composition is a composition member. A member may itself be an ISA component or may not be.
An ISA-compliant member communicates with the CIC through the ISA interface; a non-ISA member uses an interface native to that member.
The CIC is the access point for all composition capabilities exposed to the network, including tasks, published observations and reported properties.
Composition-level capabilities may combine those of the CIC and members, alongside individually provided capabilities.
A CIC can expose capabilities with or without making the member’s existence visible, regardless of whether the member is ISA-compliant.

Making a member visible entails announcing its availability, declaring its capabilities and periodically reporting its status; its communicated data/information is represented as originating at that member.
For an opaque member, the CIC does not announce the member and represents any exposed member capabilities as provided by the CIC.
A non-ISA member made visible is a virtual ISA component. Its assigned ISA identifier includes its CIC’s identifier, associating the two.
For a received external task, the CIC may perform it directly, broker it by actively tasking members, or relay it by forwarding to a target over ISA or the member’s native interface.
Only visible members can be targeted from outside the composition. A visible member whose tasking the CIC enables is transparent; if the CIC does not enable its tasking, it is translucent.
limitations: Composition, member and CIC are integration/representation meanings; their use does not establish physical enclosure, mechanical containment, cable topology or one device per member.
A CIC role need not be a Controller role. A member can be ISA-compliant without being externally visible, and virtual does not mean an ISA-compliant component or an OS virtual machine.
The containing identifier statement does not specify a new serialized UCI format, parsing rule or physical parent relation; retain the earlier UCI evidence.
Opaque does not mean that all member capabilities are absent from the network; exposed capabilities can be attributed to the CIC.
Visibility, external taskability, declared support, caller authorization, task receipt, actual execution and successful effects must not be collapsed.
Performer, broker and relay are possible roles for a given request, not an exhaustive physical taxonomy or demonstrated runtime actions.
Figure 2’s incoming Member B tasks label does not resolve the text’s translucency rule or show B executing those tasks; preserve the source tension.

records.title: Deployment Architecture
records.source_span_text:
4.3      Deployment Architecture
As described in Architecture Drivers 4.1, ISA is designed to be a distributed architecture in
order to achieve fault tolerance and autonomy, and an interconnected architecture in order
to enable wide-scale access to observation data, capability and state information, services,
and taskable components. Hence, ISA is designed to support a deployment involving
potentially many ISA Controllers, though a deployment could have as few as a single ISA
Controller.

Since an ISA component that is not an ISA Controller must connect to a Controller in order
to leverage ISA, it is essential that an ISA Controller be accessible to an ISA component.
Because access to another platform is never guaranteed in a tactical operating
environment, by default, an ISA Controller should be deployed on every tactical
platform on/in which one or more ISA-compliant systems reside. In contrast, because




                                                                                               12
 communication between platforms is much more reliable in an enterprise domain, the
distribution extent for ISA Controllers would likely instead be driven by performance
factors, such as processing load.

Systems involved in interoperability in a tactical domain will reside in/on a wide array of
types of platforms, including command posts (at all echelons), mounted ground vehicles,
aerial vehicles (unmanned aerial vehicles, manned planes, aerostats), and mobile handheld
devices. In a large-scale tactical deployment, there could be thousands of tactical platforms
of these varying types collectively hosting many thousands of systems involved in
interoperability.

The implication is that thousands of ISA Controllers could be deployed for large-scale
tactical deployments, with each Controller serving one to several ISA components. Every
ISA Controller could not connect to every other ISA Controller to share information and
data in such a deployment, nor would that be desirable if even possible given that only a
small percentage of ISA-compliant systems are likely to care about any given ISA-compliant
system in a large deployment. Instead, in-depth analysis is required to determine the
connectivity and information/data-sharing between ISA Controllers that would yield the
optimal balance between meeting soldiers’ operational needs and minimizing bandwidth
consumption (as well as, secondarily, processing resource consumption). ISA Controllers
support both static configurations and dynamic mechanisms for identifying the other ISA
Controllers with which interconnection is needed.




                                                                                              13
records.meaning: Describes distributed Controller placement and interconnection choices under tactical and enterprise operating assumptions, without prescribing a physical equipment hierarchy.
native_rules: A deployment can contain many Controllers or as few as one.
A non-Controller ISA component needs access to a Controller to use ISA.
By default an ISA Controller should be deployed on every tactical platform on/in which ISA-compliant systems reside, because access to another platform is not guaranteed.
In an enterprise domain the expected better cross-platform communication means distribution is more likely driven by performance factors such as processing load.
Large-scale scenarios may involve thousands of platforms and Controllers; the source does not propose every Controller connecting to every other Controller.

Controller interconnection needs analysis to balance information needs, bandwidth and processing cost; Controllers support static configurations and dynamic mechanisms for identifying needed interconnections.
limitations: Preserve should and by default. This tactical recommendation is not a universal requirement for every physical platform or a rule that all systems share one Controller.
Thousands is a hypothetical scale illustration, not a measured deployment, a tested capacity, a limit or an exact component-to-Controller cardinality.
The document calls for analysis but does not provide an optimized topology, performance benchmark or automatically complete information-sharing guarantee.
Hosting and communications do not prove physical part-of or actual controlled-case deployment details.

5.0 Services
 Core ISA services are ISA services that are required to be part of every ISA deployment.

 The core ISA services for ISA 6.0 are:

    1. Communication Service

    2. Authorization Service

    3. Live Data Service.

 Each ISA 6.0 Controller will typically provide the Communication Service and the Live Data
 Service.

 Figure 3 illustrates the communication relationships amongst the core ISA services within
 an ISA Controller, and between the core ISA services and other ISA components. As shown,
 the ISA interface is used for all of these communications. Also illustrated is that the
 Communication Service is the keystone service, serving as an endpoint for all ISA
 communications with and within an ISA Controller. The Authorization Service and Live
 Data Service are designed to communicate with the Communication Service like any ISA
 component would, initiating a connection and performing client-side behaviors. This
 design anticipates that, in a future release of ISA, the Authorization Service and Live Data
 Service might interface with a Communication Service running within a different ISA
 Controller.




                                                                                                14
 Figure 3 - Core ISA Services

records.title: Communication Service
records.source_locator: ISA Software Design Document6.0r5, section5.1.1 Communication Service; PDFpages [23, 24], printed start15
records.source_span_text:
5.1.1       Communication Service
The Communication Service is the most fundamental ISA service, providing a connection
point for ISA components, routing ISA messages (i.e., application messages exchanged over
the ISA interface), and coordinating usage of the other ISA services. The service enables
components to join an ISA network so that they can find, and be found by, other
components and to use ISA services to obtain the information and data needed.

The Communication Service provides the following key functionality:

    •   Controller discovery – Advertises the availability of the hosting ISA Controller and
        detects other ISA Controllers.

    •   Connection management – Manages the creation, maintenance, and termination of
        secure connections with other ISA components, and the negotiation of the data
        format (encoding and data model version) to be used for the connection.

    •   Registration – Manages and reports the joining and leaving of the ISA network,
        including authorization of joining (via the Authorization Service).



                                                                                               15
    •    Authentication – Determines if a joining ISA component is who it claims to be. The
        claimed identity of an ISA component is provided to the Communication Service
        during the registration process.

   •    Configuration management – Exchanges ISA capability declarations and related
        state information with each connected ISA component. ISA capability declarations
        are descriptions of the following: the information that a component can publish
        about the observations that it can make (observables), the property information for
        itself that a component can report (properties), and the commands that a
        component can be requested to execute (commands). The full set of declarations for
        a component is called a CCD. For each declared capability, a component reports a
        ready state and, if relevant, a reporting state. The ISA capabilities for ISA 6.0 are
        defined in the ISA DMS.

   •    Status reporting – Exchanges the values of declared properties with each connected
        ISA component. This exchange occurs upon configuration and periodically.

   •    Availability monitoring – Monitors the ongoing availability of registered ISA
        components, takes corrective action when components become non-responsive, and
        reports any changes to availability. Availability is based on receipt of periodic status
        reports.

   •    Request handling – Checks authorization of received requests (via the Authorization
        Service) and forwards the requests and their responses to their destination,
        including for requests destined for ISA services and joined components.

   •    Message routing – Directs ISA messages to their destinations, which could be
        another ISA component or another service within the same ISA Controller.
records.hash_basis: SHA256 of exact UTF-8 nonoverlapping pdftotext-layout span supplied by root, including original form-feed page breaks; figures separately visually inspected.
records.meaning: Defines nine Communication Service responsibilities spanning Controller discovery, secure connection management, registration/authentication, declaration/state exchange, heartbeat-based availability, request authorization/forwarding, and message routing.
native_rules: Controller discovery advertises the hosting Controller and detects other Controllers.
Connection management creates, maintains and terminates secure connections and negotiates encoding and data-model version.
Registration manages/reports joining and leaving the network, using Authorization Service for join authorization.
Authentication determines whether a joining component is who it claims to be; the claimed identity is supplied during registration.

Configuration management exchanges CCD capability declarations and related states. Capabilities describe supported observables, properties and commands; ready state is reported for each, and reporting state where relevant.
Status reporting exchanges declared property values upon configuration and periodically.
Availability monitoring uses receipt of periodic status reports, takes corrective action for nonresponsive components, and reports changes.
Request handling uses Authorization Service to check received requests and forwards requests and responses to services or joined components.

records.title: Live Data Service
records.source_locator: ISA Software Design Document6.0r5, section5.1.3 Live Data Service; PDFpages [25, 26], printed start17
records.source_span_text:
5.1.3     Live Data Service
The Live Data Service provides access to information regarding the availability, status, and
capabilities of ISA components, and to observation data produced by ISA components in
support of SA. The Live Data Service provides access via two mechanisms: discovery
queries and subscriptions.

When an ISA component submits capability information and status to the Communication
Service, the information is routed to the Live Data Service, which maintains it until a
component leaves the ISA network. The Live Data Service enables ISA components to make
discovery queries against this current information. The service compares the criteria
specified in an authorized query (e.g., all components within a certain Area of Interest
(AOI) that support a particular command) against the maintained information and returns
the matching information. If requested in the discovery query, the Live Data Service also
provides the identities of any matched ISA components. The Live Data Service supports a
rich language for specifying discovery query criteria.

ISA components can also gain access to future information and data. The Live Data Service
enables ISA components to request the creation of subscriptions, which specify the ISA
messages desired by the component. In support of filtering the information to be received,
the Live Data Service provides a rich language for defining subscription criteria. ISA
components can subscribe to messages containing status and capability information and
availability notifications (e.g., component just joined/left ISA network, component has
become unresponsive) for other components. They can also subscribe to messages
containing observation data produced by other ISA components, which could be in a raw
form (e.g., entity detection) or refined/fused in some way (e.g., correlated track). Upon
creation of a subscription, an ISA component receives the messages containing current
status and capability information for available components that match the subscription
criteria. If a subscription includes an AOI, the subscribing component will also receive
notifications when a matching component enters and exits the AOI.



                                                                                             17
 As subscribable messages are routed to it by the Communication Service, the Live Data
Service determines which subscriptions match the messages and sends them to each
matching subscriber. Hence, the subscription mechanism enables an ISA component to
receive desired information/data as soon as it becomes available, which is critical to SA.
Subscriptions can be canceled by a subscriber and are canceled by the Live Data Service
when a subscriber leaves the ISA network.

The Communication Service invokes the Authorization Service to authorize discover
queries, subscription creations, and subscription cancellations prior to forwarding the
requests to the Live Data Service.

records.title: Discovering ISA
records.source_locator: ISA Software Design Document6.0r5, section6.1 Discovering ISA; PDFpages [27], printed start19
records.source_span_text:
6.1     Discovering ISA
Before an ISA component can join an ISA network via an ISA Controller, or an ISA
Controller can interconnect with another Controller, it must obtain the network
information needed to connect to the Controller. Network information can be obtained
from a local configuration or via a dynamic mechanism.

To achieve dynamic Controller discovery, ISA employs the Zero Configuration Networking
(Zeroconf) standard, which leverages Multicast Domain Name Service (mDNS). Zeroconf is
used to periodically multicast an ISA Controller’s network information for receipt by ISA
components (including other Controllers) listening on a pre-defined multicast address.
This multicasting begins when a Controller starts up and continues until the Controller
shuts down. This use of Zeroconf facilitates discovery of Controllers as they become
available, which can change often in a tactical domain.

Zeroconf can also be used by ISA components to multicast queries to discover ISA
Controllers’ network information. ISA listens for the queries and responds with the
network information upon receipt. This use of Zeroconf by an ISA component expedites
discovery of available ISA Controllers upon startup and upon loss of connectivity to a
Controller.

In both dynamic cases, an ISA component could receive network information from multiple
ISA Controllers. When this happens, a component might need to decide which ISA
Controller is the best one with which to establish a connection (e.g., based on network
proximity).

Details regarding ISA’s support of Zeroconf are provided in the ISA ICD.

Components, including other Controllers, can listen for advertisements and can multicast discovery queries to which ISA responds with network information.
Receiving information from multiple Controllers may require selecting a preferred Controller; network proximity is an example criterion.
Detailed Zeroconf support is referred to the ISA ICD; this cross-reference is recorded, not followed in this delivery.

records.title: Connecting to ISA
records.source_locator: ISA Software Design Document6.0r5, section6.2 Connecting to ISA; PDFpages [27, 28], printed start19
records.source_span_text:
6.2     Connecting to ISA
When an ISA component decides to connect to the Controller, the component uses the ISA
interface to establish the connection and for communications over the connection. As




                                                                                            19
 previously highlighted, the low bandwidth, indeterminate connectivity, and high packet
loss/corruption characteristic of the DDIL networks that are common in the tactical
domain can drastically hamper communications between platforms. In order to enable
effective communication in such an environment, the ISA interface uses reliable protocols
and supports network-efficient encoding options. Furthermore, the ISA interface employs
communication technologies that ensure sufficient cybersecurity in all domains.

The communication technologies supported for connecting to ISA 6.0 are as follows:

   •   Networking – Internet Protocol (IP) v4 and v6

   •   Transport – Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

   •   Security – Transport Layer Security (TLS). This solution achieves endpoint
       authentication, confidentiality, and non-repudiation.

Upon establishing a secure connection, the ISA component and ISA Controller negotiate the
presentation format to be used for the ISA messages exchanged over the connection. The
presentation format is a combination of the technology for encoding the messages and the
data model schema that defines the message content. The encoding technologies supported
for ISA 6.0 are Google Protocol Buffers, which is designed for network efficiency, and the
Extensible Markup Language (XML). The data model schema is a version of the ISA Data
Model, as defined in the ISA DMS.

The negotiation of the presentation format is accomplished via the ISA Presentation Layer
(IPL). Once a presentation format is agreed upon, the ISA component and ISA Controller
can begin to exchange ISA messages. This exchange is also accomplished via the IPL. Details
for the IPL are specified in the ISA ICD.

6.3.2      ISA Lifecycle
ISA has an established lifecycle that must be followed in order to correctly participate in an
ISA network. When an ISA component initiates a connection to an ISA Controller, the
component follows this lifecycle for the remainder of the connection.

The ISA lifecycle is divided into several phases. Each phase dictates how to enter the phase,
what the ISA component must and may do while within the phase and allowed transitions
to other phases. Table 5 describes entrance criteria for, and the required and allowed
activities within, each phase. Illustrations of typical and atypical transitions between
phases follow the table.




                                                                                             25

Figure 5 presents the typical transition paths between lifecycle phases, in terms of what
message causes the transition. As described in Table 2, it is possible for other transitions to
occur, due to decisions of the ISA component or communications from the ISA Controller.


Figure 5 - Typical ISA Lifecycle Phase Transition




Figure 6 illustrates the possible, but atypical, phase transitions. All of the possible

including for error scenarios, are presented in 6.3.3 Message Flows.
